title: Chemical Coordination and Integration
description: Grade 11 Biology: the endocrine system and hormones, the major endocrine glands and their hormones, the mechanism of hormone action, and hormonal disorders.

topics.title: The Endocrine System and Hormones
topics.concept:
Besides the fast nervous system, the body has a second, slower control system — the endocrine system — that coordinates activities using chemicals called hormones. A hormone is a chemical messenger, made in a gland and carried by the blood to a distant part of the body, where it controls some activity. Hormones work in very small amounts and bring about slower but longer-lasting effects than nerves.

The glands that make hormones are the endocrine glands, also called ductless glands because they pour their secretions directly into the blood (unlike exocrine glands such as salivary or sweat glands, which release their products through ducts). The nervous system and the endocrine system work together to keep the body coordinated — this combined control is the basis of the chapter's title, "integration."

The chief difference between nervous and chemical (hormonal) coordination:

  • Nervous — uses electrical impulses along neurons; very fast, acts on specific points, and the effect is short-lived.
  • Hormonal — uses chemicals carried in blood; slower to act, can affect many parts at once, and the effect lasts longer.

Together these two systems control growth, development, metabolism, reproduction and the body's response to stress, keeping the internal environment balanced (homeostasis).

examples.solution:
It is a chemical messenger.

  • A hormone is a chemical made in a gland.
  • It is carried by the blood to a target part, where it controls an activity.
examples.answer: A hormone is a chemical messenger made in a gland and carried by the blood to control an activity in a distant part.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why are endocrine glands called ductless glands?
examples.solution:
Compare with exocrine glands.

  • They pour their secretions directly into the blood, not through a duct.
examples.answer: Because they release their hormones directly into the blood, without ducts.

examples.problem: Example 3: State two differences between nervous and hormonal coordination.
examples.solution:
Compare speed and duration.

  • Nervous: fast, electrical, short-lived effect.
  • Hormonal: slower, chemical (blood), longer-lasting effect.
examples.answer: Nervous control is fast and short-lived (electrical); hormonal control is slower and longer-lasting (chemicals in blood).

recap:
• Endocrine system: coordination by hormones (chemical messengers carried in blood, active in tiny amounts).
  • Made by endocrine (ductless) glands; release into blood (vs exocrine = ducts).
  • Nervous = fast, electrical, short; hormonal = slow, chemical, long-lasting.
  • Together = integration → control growth, metabolism, reproduction, homeostasis.

quiz.q: A hormone is carried from the gland to its target by the:
quiz.explanation: Hormones are carried by the blood to their target organs.

quiz.q: Endocrine glands are called ductless glands because they:
options: Release secretions directly into the blood
quiz.explanation: Endocrine glands pour hormones straight into the blood, without ducts.

topics.title: The Major Endocrine Glands and Their Hormones
topics.concept:
The body has several endocrine glands, each making one or more hormones with specific jobs. The most important ones are:

  • Pituitary gland — a tiny gland at the base of the brain, called the master gland because it controls many other endocrine glands. It also makes growth hormone, which controls body growth.
  • Thyroid gland — in the neck; makes thyroxine, which controls the rate of metabolism. It needs iodine to work.
  • Pancreas — makes insulin and glucagon, which control the level of glucose (sugar) in the blood. (The pancreas is both endocrine and exocrine.)
  • Adrenal glands — on top of the kidneys; make adrenaline, the "fight-or-flight" hormone released during fear, anger or excitement (it speeds the heart and prepares the body for emergency).
  • Sex glands (gonads) — the testes make testosterone (male hormone) and the ovaries make oestrogen and progesterone (female hormones); these control sexual development and reproduction.

Two examples show how precisely hormones act: insulin lowers blood sugar after a meal, while adrenaline instantly readies the body to react to danger. The amount of each hormone is carefully controlled by feedback — if there is too much or too little, the body adjusts its release to bring it back to normal.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is the pituitary gland called the master gland?
examples.solution:
It controls other glands.

  • The pituitary controls many other endocrine glands.
  • So it is called the master gland.
examples.answer: Because it controls the working of many other endocrine glands.

examples.problem: Example 2: Which hormone controls blood sugar, and which gland makes it?
examples.solution:
Recall the sugar-controlling hormone.

  • Insulin controls blood sugar.
  • It is made by the pancreas.
examples.answer: Insulin, made by the pancreas, controls the level of glucose in the blood.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the role of adrenaline?
examples.solution:
It is the emergency hormone.

  • Adrenaline is the 'fight-or-flight' hormone.
  • It is released in fear/anger and prepares the body for emergency (e.g. faster heartbeat).
examples.answer: Adrenaline is the 'fight-or-flight' hormone that prepares the body for emergencies (e.g. speeds the heartbeat).

recap:
• Pituitary = master gland (+ growth hormone); thyroid → thyroxine (metabolism, needs iodine).
  • Pancreas → insulin/glucagon (blood sugar); adrenal → adrenaline (fight-or-flight).
  • Gonads: testes → testosterone; ovaries → oestrogen/progesterone (reproduction).
  • Hormone levels controlled by feedback.

quiz.q: The 'master gland' that controls many other endocrine glands is the:
quiz.explanation: The pituitary gland is the master gland.

quiz.q: The hormone that controls the level of glucose in the blood is:
quiz.explanation: Insulin (from the pancreas) controls blood glucose.

topics.title: Mechanism of Hormone Action and Disorders
topics.concept:
Although a hormone travels in the blood and reaches every part of the body, it only affects certain organs — its target organs. This is because the cells of the target organ carry special receptors that exactly fit that hormone (a lock-and-key arrangement). When the hormone binds its receptor, it switches on a particular response inside the cell — for example, insulin binds liver and muscle cells and makes them take in glucose from the blood. Cells without the matching receptor simply ignore the hormone. This is why a hormone produces a specific effect even though it is carried everywhere.

Because hormones must be present in just the right amount, too much or too little of a hormone causes a disorder:

  • Diabetes mellitus — too little insulin (or the body not responding to it), so blood sugar stays high; it can cause sugar in the urine and many complications. It is managed by diet, exercise and sometimes insulin injections.
  • Goitre — swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck, often caused by a lack of iodine in the diet (which is why we use iodised salt).
  • Dwarfism (too little growth hormone in childhood) and gigantism (too much) — disorders of body growth.
  • Stress conditions linked to overactive adrenaline.

Understanding these disorders shows how finely the endocrine system is balanced. A healthy diet (including iodine and not too much sugar), regular exercise, and timely medical care help keep the hormones — and therefore the whole body — in balance.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why does a hormone affect only its target organ even though it travels all over the body?
examples.solution:
Only some cells can respond.

  • Only the target organ's cells have receptors that fit the hormone.
  • Cells without the matching receptor ignore it.
examples.answer: Because only the target organ's cells have the specific receptors that fit the hormone; others ignore it.

examples.solution:
It involves insulin.

  • Too little insulin (or the body not responding to it).
  • So blood sugar stays high.
examples.answer: Too little insulin (or poor response to it), causing high blood sugar.

examples.problem: Example 3: What deficiency causes goitre, and how is it prevented?
examples.solution:
It is about the thyroid.

  • Goitre is often caused by a lack of iodine.
  • It is prevented by using iodised salt.
examples.answer: A lack of iodine causes goitre; it is prevented by using iodised salt.

recap:
• A hormone acts only on its target organ, whose cells have matching receptors (lock-and-key); others ignore it.
  • Diabetes mellitus: too little insulin → high blood sugar; goitre: thyroid swelling from iodine deficiency (use iodised salt).
  • Dwarfism/gigantism: too little/much growth hormone.
  • Balanced diet, exercise and medical care keep hormones in balance.

quiz.explanation: Only the target cells have receptors that fit the hormone.

quiz.q: Goitre is commonly caused by a deficiency of:
quiz.explanation: Iodine deficiency causes goitre, prevented by iodised salt.

questions.q: Coordination using chemical messengers is done by the:
questions.explanation: The endocrine system coordinates using hormones.

questions.q: A hormone is carried from a gland to its target by the:
questions.explanation: Hormones travel in the blood to their targets.

questions.q: Endocrine glands are called ductless because they:
questions.explanation: They release hormones directly into the blood, without ducts.

questions.q: Compared with nervous control, hormonal control is:
questions.explanation: Hormonal effects are slower to start but last longer.

questions.q: The 'master gland' is the:
questions.explanation: The pituitary controls many other glands — the master gland.

questions.q: Thyroxine, which controls metabolism, is made by the:
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland makes thyroxine (needs iodine).

questions.q: Insulin and glucagon, which control blood sugar, are made by the:
questions.explanation: The pancreas makes insulin and glucagon.

questions.q: The 'fight-or-flight' hormone is:
questions.explanation: Adrenaline, from the adrenal gland, prepares the body for emergencies.

questions.q: The male sex hormone made by the testes is:
questions.explanation: The testes make testosterone.

questions.q: Growth hormone is secreted by the:
questions.explanation: The pituitary makes growth hormone.

questions.q: A hormone affects only its target organ because those cells have matching:
questions.explanation: Target cells carry specific receptors that fit the hormone.

questions.q: Too little insulin (or poor response to it) causes:
questions.explanation: Lack of effective insulin causes diabetes mellitus.

questions.q: Goitre (thyroid swelling) is usually caused by a lack of:
questions.explanation: Iodine deficiency causes goitre; iodised salt prevents it.

questions.q: Too little growth hormone in childhood causes:
questions.explanation: A shortage of growth hormone in childhood causes dwarfism.

questions.q: The amount of each hormone is kept in balance by:
questions.explanation: Feedback mechanisms keep hormone levels balanced.

questions.q: After a sugary meal, insulin lowers blood glucose mainly by causing cells to:
options: Take up glucose from the blood
questions.explanation: Insulin signals liver and muscle cells to absorb glucose, lowering its level in the blood.

questions.q: A frightened person's heart races because of a sudden release of:
questions.explanation: Adrenaline triggers the fight-or-flight response, speeding the heart.

questions.q: Adding iodine to table salt helps prevent goitre because iodine is needed to make:
questions.explanation: The thyroid needs iodine to make thyroxine; iodised salt supplies it and prevents goitre.

questions.q: Although hormones circulate everywhere, a hormone acts on just one organ because only that organ's cells have the right:
questions.explanation: Specific receptors (lock-and-key) ensure only target cells respond.

questions.q: Damage to the pituitary could disturb many body functions because it:
questions.explanation: As the master gland, the pituitary regulates other glands, so its damage has wide effects.

questions.q: Both the nervous and endocrine systems are needed because together they provide:
options: Fast short-term and slow long-term coordination
questions.explanation: Nerves give rapid brief responses and hormones give slower lasting control — together they fully coordinate the body.
